entry.title: The coming global wealth destruction
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The coming global wealth destructionThe coming global wealth destruction

Between AI-driven cyber chaos, two wars, and street mayhem, global prosperity is no longer guaranteed

premium

Rising AI-driven cyber threats, financial instability and geopolitical tensions pose growing risks to India's economic security, underscoring the need for stronger preventive measures. | Illustration : Binay Sinha

R Jagannathan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 11:42 PM ISTThe late Gen Bipin Rawat talked of the armed forces’ preparedness to take on not just a two-front threat, but a two-and-a-half-front one. The half front he referred to was the internal threat to the country’s unity and integrity. We now need to extend this analogy globally. The half-front threat is no longer limited to our subcontinent; it now confronts major countries in Europe and could possibly engulf America in the future. Only autocracies or countries with monocultural populations seem to be partly immune to this threat today, as scenes from France, Italy, Spain, Albania and elsewhere strongly suggest. The US could face its own half-front if Donald Trump’s party loses the November elections, as seems likely.  The half-front threats are not limited to visible ones alone. We now need to add the invisible ones too — the threat from artificial intelligence (AI)-driven cybercrime and fraud, the amplification of small internal problems into major ones using disinformation and AI fakes, and the most obvious one — the threat to jobs from rapid technological improvements, which are deliberately being suppressed by AI evangelists by showing us only AI’s benefits.  Once jobs are impacted in a big way, the half front will become even more aggressive than the external threats to India and many other countries. We should not ignore the debt time-bombs now being mishandled by many European countries (Greece, Italy, France among them) and some large AI companies too, which are borrowing money hand over fist — and at huge interest rates. These are running into trillions of dollars, and any bond or equity market collapse could trigger a major wealth destruction spree globally.  As I write this column this week, the cyber-threat headlines are deeply concerning: State Bank of India has just reported a large breach of customer data, which has now surfaced on the dark web; HDFC Bank is probing the leak of crucial and confidential data; a Bengaluru-based cybersecurity firm, eMudhra, apparently used weak cryptographic keys that could have allowed crooks to fake trusted digital certificates; government websites in Europe went dark after AI exposed flaws in the PHP programming language; a Chinese-speaking hacker used AI agents and tools to hack into almost 100 websites; and Japan has declared a cyber emergency after a wave of cyberattacks that led to the exposure of data on over 14 million citizens and affected over 600 corporate and public bodies. And we have not even added the rogue AI agents that our large language model companies have let loose on an unwary public.  India is simply not recognising the extent of the potential risks to our economy and national wealth posed by the two-and-a-half-front threat, aided by potentially destabilising AI-led cyber and other attacks.  India’s apex cyber protection organisation, the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), has been issuing many advisories to the public, banks and corporations about rising threats to poorly architected legacy software and hardware systems, but millions and millions of small and medium businesses, and ordinary citizens, are simply unaware or unable to do anything about it.  We quite simply have to become more paranoid about our cyber vulnerabilities, and we could begin by declaring a red alert on cyber threats, or even a cyber emergency, as Japan has done. Yes, this kind of alert or emergency will have a sharp short-term negative impact on business confidence and trust in devices and digital spaces, but it is better to be safe than sorry. The damage — like, say, a debilitating attack on a major player in the banking system — will be far greater if we choose to stay silent.  The only comfort India can draw from its own vulnerabilities is that the world is not becoming any safer, as the threats facing Europe and Japan show. But as a lower-middle-income country with millions teetering just above the poverty line, we cannot afford a major financial or economic meltdown. Or street protests that can spiral out of control. Protests over even genuine issues could end up being amplified by malignant cyber warriors, attracting lumpen elements that may end up damaging property and businesses, as we are seeing in Europe.  This is happening when the world’s most powerful countries are unable to end two wars that are pushing up living costs for the vulnerable, which will only make the internal half-fronts more volatile. This is not the time for any country, especially democratic ones, to fetishise street protests in the name of liberal values when these could spill over into something worse. In Albania, angry crowds hurled petrol bombs at government buildings and set fire to the Supreme Court.  When we put all these things together, we should come to the following conclusions: One, we are just a few political and economic missteps away from setting off a major wealth destruction spiral globally that will dwarf the 2008 global financial crisis; two, the threats to jobs and livelihoods will accelerate the downward spiral if we allow things to get worse on the streets.  The message for India and the world is simple: First, fix and defuse the domestic half-front through dialogue and strong preventive action (one is not a substitute for the other); second, bring the two unfinished wars to an end even if it implies that underlying issues have not been resolved; and third, start work on reforming global institutions, if necessary by creating trustworthy systems outside what the Big Two are willing to accept.  Whether it is the United Nations or the World Trade Organization or the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, the era of Western hegemony is clearly coming to an end, and even the West is not on the same page anymore.  Europe, in particular, is splintering, and the political middle everywhere is being outgunned by those on the Left or Right. The old so-called “liberal” order has become a pale shadow of itself, degenerating into a caricature. Any liberal democracy that seeks to cancel the Right or Left will end up cancelling the workable middle position where compromises are possible. In India, the Left occupies the intellectual and elite spaces, while the Right (assuming we can call the Bharatiya Janata Party right-wing, which is far from reality) occupies many formal positions of power. The two need to make peace.  Solutions need consensus, and a consensus cannot be forged by silencing or cancelling voices that may not agree with you. The street will not, however, provide any better answers.

entry.title: From tathastu to delulu
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / From tathastu to deluluFrom tathastu to delulu

From Sanskritised Hindi to Gen Z slang, India's language is shifting from formal expressions of authority to relatable words shaped by social media, memes and emotions.

premium

Social media and meme culture are reshaping how young Indians communicate, with expressions such as 'delulu', 'rizz' and 'slay' gaining popularity. (Photo: Freepik)

Sandeep Goyal4 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 11:01 PM ISTYou didn’t say development, you said vikas. You didn’t say support, you said samarthan. You didn’t say inclusive, you said sarva-samaveshi.  Every government scheme, every newspaper editorial, every college debate was an exercise in competitive sanskritisation. The more syllables you could add from Sanskrit, the more serious you sounded.  “Rashtriya Ekta Ka Sankalp”, “Antyodaya Se Sarvodaya”, and “Garib Kalyan Aur Utthan Yojana”.  If you couldn’t pronounce it in one breath, it must be important.  That era is over. It didn’t end with a notification. It ended with a 19-year-old on Instagram saying “I’m so delulu”.  Welcome to the Great Lexicon Flip: The old words wanted respect. The new words want relatability. For 70 years, our public language was designed to make you feel small. Politicians, editors, professors spoke in shuddh Hindi, heavy Sanskrit, and clipped English — language that said: I know more than you, so listen.  The scheme is not for poor people, it’s for “Antyodaya”. You are not poor, you are “Alp-aay varg”. You didn’t fail, you are “Asafal”. The words were curtains, meant to keep you at a respectful distance. Then Gen Z came and tore the curtains.  Delulu. No cap. Slay. Rizz. Ick. Vibe check. Main character energy. Touch grass. These words are not trying to impress you. They are trying to include you. They are three seconds long, they are feelings, not definitions. You don’t need a dictionary, you need a mood.  Delulu is the best example. What does delulu mean? Delusional. But saying “delusional” sounds clinical, like a doctor is about to show up. Saying “I’m delulu” sounds cute, self-aware, funny. I know I’m being unrealistic about my crush, my career, my life, but I’m enjoying it. It’s delusion with a wink.  In one word, an entire generation has turned self-awareness into a joke, and the joke into a coping mechanism. No Sanskrit word could ever do that. “Aatm-mugdh bhram” will never trend.  Basically, Sanskrit words told you what to do. Gen Z words tell you how you feel. This is the core shift. The old lexicon was imperative, moral, top-down. Karya, kartavya, nishtha, sankalp, anushasan. Do your duty. Take a pledge. Be disciplined.  The new lexicon is emotional, diagnostic, sideways. I have the ick. He has no rizz. That gave me anxiety. I’m in my flop era.  Old language told you how to behave in society. New language tells you how to name what society did to you. We have moved from a nation of do-ers to a nation of feel-ers. And the words had to change.  A boy in 1985 who liked a girl would be told “Sanyam rakho”. A boy in 2025 says, “I’m so down bad for her, I’m full delulu, but she has rizz.”  Same emotion, completely different processing. The first one represses, the second one posts a story.  Why is Sanskrit losing out? Because it can’t be abbreviated. This is a technical problem. Internet language is built for speed. You can’t shorten “Sarvabhaumikaran” but you can shorten “delusional” to “delulu”. You can’t shorten “Sahridayata” but you can say “that’s so wholesome”. You can’t type “Atmanirbhar” quickly, but you can type “slay”.  Gen Z language is made for thumbs. Sanskritised language was made for tongues that had time. It needed a stage, a mic, an audience that would wait. Gen Z language needs seven seconds on a reel before you swipe.  And more importantly, Gen Z words are remixable. You can be delulu. You can have delulu is the solulu — delusion is the solution. You can be in delulu land. Try doing that with “Aatm-nirbharta”. “Aatm-nirbharta is the solulu”? It dies on your lips.  Delulu works because it can become a meme, a sticker, a caption, a T-shirt. Sanskrit words could only become a slogan on a government wall. Sanskritised Hindi wanted to make India sound ancient and serious. Delulu language wants to make India sound young and not-so-serious, because being serious has not helped anyway. Embrace “skibidi” a word with multiple meanings: It can mean “cool”, “bad”, or just be used as a joke. You will be hearing a lot of it in the days ahead.  And honestly? It’s more honest. Saying “I’m delulu but I have main character energy” is a more accurate description of middle-class Indian life right now than “Mera sankalp viksit Bharat hai”.  We are a nation that is delusional about many things — jobs, love, Canada visa, crypto — and the only solution is indeed delusion. Delulu is the solulu. At least the kids have named it right.  
 The writer is chairman, Rediffusion.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Gen Z BS Opinion Sanskrit language Indian languages Social Media memes

entry.title: In Nitish Kumar's name and his caste base
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / In Nitish Kumar's name and his caste baseIn Nitish Kumar's name and his caste base

Speculation over renaming the JD(U) and a possible merger with the BJP has intensified questions about Nitish Kumar's political legacy and the party's future in Bihar.

premium

Nitish Kumar's political succession remains uncertain as competing factions within the JD(U) debate the party's future and its relationship with the BJP. (Photo:PTI)

Aditi Phadnis5 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 10:42 PM ISTA sure sign that something is amiss in a political party is when its members start saying its name should be changed.  The move to change a name usually heralds a split.  In the Janata Dal (United), or JD(U), this discussion started last month, when its National Working President Sanjay Jha said at Khagaria, Bihar: “The time has come to change the name of the JD(U) to Janata Dal (Nitish).” The refrain was taken up immediately by Shrawan Kumar, a Kurmi leader considered a claimant to the caste capital Nitish Kumar represents, and Bijendra Kumar Yadav, current deputy chief minister of Bihar and a man who has represented the same constituency (Supaul) for nine terms without a break.  As Nitish Kumar battles health problems and a legacy that combines a formidable caste coalition, good governance and the politics of opportunism, many in the party are eyeing the corner office in the belief that they would be better placed to control the trajectory of Bihar politics if they can get their hands on this weapon. They haven’t reckoned with the sense of political discernment of the average Bihari.  Bihar’s caste survey tells us that the Other Backward Classes (OBCs) and Extremely Backward Classes (EBCs) make up nearly 63 per cent of the state’s 140 million people. Those in the general category (forward castes like Brahmins and Bhumihars) are just around 15 per cent. Naturally, with this kind of social composition, Bihar’s caste politics is quite different from that of Uttar Pradesh (UP), where upper castes range between 18 and 22 per cent of the population. In UP, upper castes are numerous enough to matter in a political equation. In Bihar, backward-caste combinations count more.  Nitish Kumar grasped this early on, mastering and playing with the complexity of social coalitions. His greatest contribution to Bihar politics was forcing all political players to accept the reality and enduring presence of caste, creating a playing field where ignoring caste was at their own peril. Lalu Prasad had already tapped into the OBC vein and extended the coalition to include Muslims. Nitish Kumar offered shelter to those below the OBCs and, frequently, their victims: The EBCs, including lower castes among the Muslims. The BJP tried hard to offer lofty ideals to replace caste identity. But it met with limited electoral success. With Nitish Kumar/JD(U)’s base, it could manage the numbers to form a government.  But if Nitish Kumar and Lalu Prasad were to join up, the BJP, despite its appeal to nationalism and Hindutva, would find itself in the opposition space. Its discomfort with caste identity — as Arun Jaitley had told Business Standard once — made it a camp for forward castes. And when Nitish Kumar’s EBC base joined it, it became an unbeatable combination.  Over the years, while castes have migrated to the Bharatiya Janata Party, the biggest chunk of EBCs has remained loyal to Nitish Kumar and the JD(U). For the BJP, this is a problem. When the EBCs and the OBCs — Nitish Kumar and Lalu Prasad — come together, the BJP finds itself elbowed out as it found in 2013 and 2022, when Nitish Kumar walked out of the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) and joined up with Lalu Prasad.  In the 2015 Assembly polls, the Lalu-Nitish combine won a handsome victory (178 of the 243 Assembly seats). But Nitish Kumar returned to the NDA in 2017. The result of his walkout again in 2022 and his subsequent return to the NDA may have confused the chatterati outside Bihar. In Bihar, it burnished, especially among his caste base, his credentials as kingmaker. In the 2025 Assembly elections, the BJP got 89 seats, still short of forming a government on its own. But with Nitish Kumar (85 seats) and other groups, the coalition reached 202.  All this points to one inescapable conclusion: The JD(U) with Nitish Kumar still has a base among EBCs. If this base decamps to Lalu Prasad, the BJP could be in trouble, and for that reason, the JD(U) needs to continue to exist and stay in the NDA tent. In Bihar, the project to supplant caste with Hindu nationalism is still incomplete.  This could be one reason why the BJP has made no energetic efforts to break the JD(U) and win over JD(U) leaders as it is trying to do in Maharashtra with the Ajit Pawar group of the ruling coalition in the state. Some JD(U) leaders like Sanjay Jha realise this. But others like Rajiv Ranjan Singh (Lalan Singh), who is a minister in the Union government by virtue of the BJP-JD(U) coalition in the state, feel more comfortable with the BJP. Indeed, Lalan’s presence at a press conference at the BJP headquarters alongside Piyush Goyal earlier this month sparked speculation that merger plans were afoot.  It is that speculation that the current leadership of the JD(U) is trying to scotch by seeking to call the party by a different name in the belief that invoking Nitish Kumar’s name will also invoke his legacy among his supporters. As the two tendencies battle it out in the JD(U) and the patriarch is unable to weigh in, who will inherit Nitish Kumar’s political legacy is not a settled issue yet.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Diwali, more flash than fireworks and more bang for the borrowed buck?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Diwali, more flash than fireworks and more bang for the borrowed buck?Diwali, more flash than fireworks and more bang for the borrowed buck?

From picture-perfect pujas to prosperity parades, Diwali has become a festival of faith, flexing and financial overreach

premium

Representative Picture

Ajanta Krishnamurthy5 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 9:50 PM ISTDiwali has acquired a curious extra ritual. Before the prayer, after the prayer, sometimes instead of the prayer, somebody must document the proceedings. The rangoli needs a clean shot. The mithai must look plentiful but artfully placed. The family must appear spontaneous on the count of three. Even the diya has to pull its weight.  Some people light a diya to dispel darkness. Others light it to improve their engagement rate.  I know the drill. I’ve photographed a meal before eating it and moved a bowl two inches because the light was better there. I’ve also zoomed in on strangers’ festive living rooms. Was that Italian marble? Solid brass? And was that a second living room? Meanwhile, mine had the audacity to look lived in.  The point is not that posting a photograph is a crime against civilisation. It is that the camera has quietly acquired editorial control. We arrange the evening for the image, then inhabit whatever remains. The experience and its proof have become difficult to separate. If the moment was lovely but nobody saw it, does it still count? And if a hundred people approve of the picture, must we pretend the evening was lovely?  The annual parade of prosperity is where the joke gets expensive. The Sharmas have a new car; the Bhatias have a modular kitchen; the Khannas’ necklace could be spotted from a passing aircraft. Your family has bought a pressure cooker. Sensible, useful, built to last, and socially invisible.  There is nothing wrong with wanting nice things. The exhaustion begins when every nice thing becomes a referendum on your standing. The car is no longer just transport; it is a message to the neighbour. The sofa must compete with a stranger’s living room. The phone works perfectly well, but it is two models old, which in the court of public opinion is practically a disability.  Being affluent and looking affluent are different occupations. One accumulates assets; the other accumulates monthly payments.  The EMI never appears in the photograph. Nor does the domestic negotiation that preceded the purchase, or the credit card bill waiting behind the festive filter. Two families can admire each other’s outward prosperity while financing it at punishing interest. The bank, which has no need to like or follow either family, is better placed to judge.  Instagram did not invent this competition. Our parents compared gold, scooters, curtains and television sets long before the internet arrived. The old neighbourhood had its own pecking order; it simply lacked a search bar. What has changed is the scale. The Sharmas’ holiday, a stranger’s walk-in wardrobe and an influencer’s Miele kitchen can all land in the same morning scroll. Envy no longer needs to wait for a Diwali invitation. The algorithm may know nothing about affection, but it knows exactly how long you linger over somebody else’s chandelier.  And where there is envy, there is a market. Diwali has always brought shopping with it: new clothes, gifts, sweets, utensils, gold. Buying something for someone can express affection, habit, faith or hope. The modern sales pitch goes further. It sells not just a product but the promise of a better, more enviable self. This perfume will make you desirable; this phone will make your memories worth keeping; this makeover will make you the sort of person who hosts effortlessly.  A festival associated with renewal is a marketer’s dream. Why begin again with a prayer when you can begin again with a wardrobe refresh and a limited period offer? The purchase arrives in a box. Contentment, somehow, remains on back order.  The deeper irony is that the market profits from the feeling that we are not quite enough, then sells us objects to close the gap. The objects may be lovely; the gap keeps moving. A new phone becomes old, the neighbour changes cars, and the sofa that looked luxurious last Diwali has been demoted by an algorithm. We call this aspiration. Sometimes it is simply insecurity with a shopping bag.  None of this makes Diwali fake. Its meanings vary across India’s communities and regions. For many Hindus, the festival recalls Rama’s return to Ayodhya; in other homes, Lakshmi worship and other traditions shape the celebration. Lamps, prayers, food, family and gifts carry meanings no platform can manufacture. Commerce has not erased the festival. It has simply found a way to sit at the table and serve itself the largest portion.  The awkward question is what happens when display starts dictating the celebration. A photograph of charity may draw attention to a cause, or turn another person’s hardship into a prop. A family picture can preserve affection, or demand that affection perform on cue. The same act can be sincere and self-conscious. Humans are perfectly capable of mixed motives; social media merely gives them a ring light.  Perhaps the most revealing part of the Diwali post is what it leaves out: the bill, the bickering, the tired person behind the camera, the relative who came because the invitation mattered more than the décor. None of this fits the polished story of abundance. Yet real life has always been untidy. Festivals are made of interruptions as much as rituals: burnt snacks, old jokes, prayers mumbled by someone checking the time, a box of mithai quietly disappearing.  I will probably post a photograph. I’d like to claim otherwise, but virtue is much easier when nobody is watching. Still, I might let the evening get on with itself before asking it to prove it happened.  The phone can have a picture. It need not have the final word.

entry.title: Are works of fiction really all fiction?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Are works of fiction really all fiction?Are works of fiction really all fiction?

Fiction offers more than entertainment, opening windows to new worlds, building knowledge and keeping the reading habit alive amid digital distractions

premium

Books by Arthur Hailey, for instance, used to be so well researched that each of them gave a young reader a window to a new world

Ambi Parameswaran6 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 12:11 AM ISTThe news item about the passing away of the British writer Jeffrey Archer caught my attention (October 7, Business Standard). It also reminded me of the many occasions where I got to listen to him, in Mumbai and Jaipur. His books have sold millions of copies in India and I am told he wanted his books to hit the bookshops in India early to scupper the plans of pirated copy makers.  Jeffery Archer, with others like John Grisham and Dan Brown, brought back young people into reading English fiction. In order to understand the changing habits of youngsters with respect to popular culture, I usually do a survey among my students at the S P Jain Institute of Management and Research: What they read (fiction/ non-fiction); what they watch; what they listen to etc.  What surprises me is the range of fiction books they read. Some of them mention Harry Potter to be the last fiction book they have read.  That aside, I see Dan Brown, Jeffrey Archer, John Grisham, Amitava Ghosh, Amish, Chetan Bhagat. I also see books like The Kite Runner, Kafka on the Shore; even some old classics like Animal Farm and Brothers Karmazov. In a class of 80, I often get at least 50 distinct names mentioned. Very few get multiple mentions.  I wonder — if someone had done a similar survey in the late 1970s or ’80s, would we have got such divergent choice of books? Remember the question is very specific: Which is the last fiction book you have read?  We keep hearing that the book reading habit is dying. Bookshops are shutting down. Physical books are on their way out. A lot of that is true. There is just a lot more content out there. In the form of social media posts and Insta reels. The fight for consumer attention has never been more fierce. It is only getting more intense with AI Slop ruling the waves.  The signs are everywhere. As a school student, in the 1970s, growing up in Chennai, I was a regular at all the local libraries — the Central Library, the British Council Library, etc. But my favourite was the Easwari Lending Library. It started as an old paper mart but became a library that kids and elders used to throng.  A few years ago I had the opportunity to spend some time at the very same library. It is now being run by the founder Palani’s son. They still have a great collection. And have multiple branches across Chennai including dedicated libraries in gated communities. But I was told that except for the weekends, they don’t have the kind of crowds they used to have a few decades ago. While they have several thousand members, most of them don’t visit too often. Even when they come, they don’t borrow too many books. One other interesting trivia that he shared was that with kids, there is often a reading wave. Some authors will trend for a few years. Only to fade away. Unlike the B School students we saw, school students seem to be reading fiction books in groups. So if you did the same survey among 80 school students in say Class 9 you may get only 10 titles as the last fiction book read.  Why does reading fiction matter? Even for a business school student?  I remember a business leader, the CEO of a large company, a voracious reader no less, who introduced me to the book On War by Carl von Clausewitz, telling me proudly that he never read fiction. I did not want to tell him why he should start reading fiction but I got an answer in a talk that author Amitav Ghosh gave a few years ago at one of his book launches. He said that when Leo Tolstoy was writing his magnum opus War and Peace he thought he was writing history. It turned out to be, what we call, historical fiction. In a similar vein, Amitav Ghosh explained, his series of books, The Ibis Trilogy, are deeply researched to the extent they are historically accurate, but are fiction all the same.  Books by Arthur Hailey, for instance, used to be so well researched that each of them gave a young reader a window to a new world. The world of hospitals, or airports for instance.  Reading books by Jeffrey Archer gave us a window to the world of British politics, banking, nobility and more. John Grisham gave us a window to the world of law. Then there are those books that are sheer reading pleasure and nostalgia. You can put R K Narayan at the top of that list.  How to find the time to dive into fiction in our busy busy world? Some friends of mine have gone fully audio. They use their morning walk to listen to a book. Some others have opted for the digital version of books, sampling them on their ride home. I am sure if you see value you will find the time. In my mind it is a misnomer to classify all works of fiction as just time-pass. Let me share an interesting incident about books. Fiction.  I was on a flight back from Kochi to Mumbai. I had the latest Tom Clancy book for company and was immersed in it. Next to me was a smart young person who was observing me keenly. After a bit, he asked me: Do you read these heavy Tom Clancy books? I told him I do and I find them unputdownable. And greatly educative. To that he said he was with the Indian Navy and with the Southern Naval Command based in Kochi. It is a major operational and training hub. He told me that Tom Clancy’s books were recommended reading for every trainee.  We then got into an interesting discussion about how much research must have gone into even fiction books. By the time I landed in Mumbai my belief in reading fiction was further strengthened.

entry.title: Navigating Europe's regulatory maze
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Navigating Europe's regulatory mazeNavigating Europe's regulatory maze

Market access to the EU is shifting from tariff barriers to regulatory requirements

premium

Tighter EU trade and sustainability rules are raising compliance costs and reshaping market access for Indian exporters

Sangeeth SelvarajuPrachi Priya5 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 10:37 PM ISTThe European Union’s recent decision to tighten steel import restrictions highlights the emerging shifts in the global trade landscape. From July 2026, the EU replaced its existing steel safeguard regime with a new framework that reduced duty-free tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) by roughly 47 per cent and increased the out-of-quota duty from 25 per cent to 50 per cent. The new framework also expanded the range of steel product categories covered and introduced stricter traceability requirements, including “melt-and-pour” reporting, which requires importers to identify where the steel was originally melted and cast. By June 30, 2027, the European Commission will assess whether the framework’s scope should be extended to downstream goods manufactured from steel or containing significant amounts of it.   The steel TRQ decision is only one part of a broader European regulatory “spaghetti bowl” that includes the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR), Digital Product Passports, the EU Deforestation Regulation, REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals), the Battery Regulation and new waste shipment rules.  While each measure may be justified on environmental, consumer protection or industrial policy grounds, together they are reshaping market access by linking trade more closely to carbon performance, product sustainability, supply-chain due diligence and traceability. For exporters, the challenge is no longer just tariffs, but navigating an increasingly dense web of regulatory compliance.   These measures affect exporters in different ways. Some act as border measures, directly impacting exporter entry into the EU market (such as CBAM, steel tariff-rate quotas ). Others are product-specific requirements that must be met before goods can be sold in Europe (such as ESPR, Digital Product Passports, REACH and the Battery Regulation). A third category operates through supply-chain regulations, such as the CSRD and CSDDD, which require European companies to obtain detailed information on sustainability, emissions and traceability from suppliers worldwide.  Alongside these measures is the EU’s extensive framework of technical regulations and standards, including REACH, CE marking for European conformity, packaging and product safety requirements. Though less visible than CBAM, they can act as barriers through testing, certification, documentation and ongoing compliance obligations.  Perhaps the least discussed but most revealing example is the revised EU Waste Shipment Regulation. The EU has tightened controls on exports of waste, particularly to non- Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries, unless those countries can demonstrate environmentally sound waste management systems. The regulation affects scrap traders, recyclers and processors. While framed as an environmental measure, it can effectively retain critical low-carbon raw materials within Europe. For aluminium and steel producers, this can reduce scrap availability, increase costs for producers elsewhere, and complicate decarbonisation efforts. Europe is, therefore, not only regulating products entering its market but also shaping access to the materials needed to produce them.  Viewed together, these measures represent a fundamental shift in the nature of trade barriers. A steel or aluminium exporter may need to provide emissions data under CBAM, sustainability disclosures for CSRD or CSDDD through value chain, product-level information under ESPR, compliance declarations under REACH, and traceability records under sector-specific regulations. This is before considering TRQs, anti-dumping measures, conformity assessments and other technical standards. Even if free-trade agreements or FTAs reduce tariffs to zero, exporters will still need to navigate this increasingly complex regulatory architecture. Market access, therefore, is shifting from tariff barriers to regulatory requirements.  For India, the priority is to institutionalise engagement with the EU, rather than respond to regulations one by one. First, the government should establish an inter-ministerial coordination mechanism to monitor emerging EU regulations and assess their implications for India. Given that these measures increasingly cut across sectors and ministries, including commerce, power, new & renewable energy, steel, mines, heavy industries and environment, a coordinated platform involving relevant ministries and industry bodies would help develop informed positions and ensure timely engagement with the EU during the EU consultation process.  Second,  India should use the India–EU FTA to establish a formal regulatory cooperation mechanism, such as an India-EU Regulatory Help Desk. Such a platform (with representation from industry bodies) could provide early notification of proposed regulations with significant trade implications, facilitate dialogue on standards, and MRV (measurement, reporting and verification) procedures, promote the recognition of equivalent measures where appropriate, and advocate reasonable transition periods for compliance.  Third, India should develop a mechanism to calculate the actual compliance and trade costs of EU regulations by collecting data on certification costs, compliance time, rejected or delayed consignments, and their impact on industries, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This evidence-based approach would strengthen India’s engagement with the EU and its participation in committees of the World Trade Organization.  Fourth, India should build issue-specific coalitions with other developing countries to engage with the EU on regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens. The objective should not be to oppose sustainability goals, but to ensure that their implementation takes into account differences in levels of economic development, technical expertise and institutional capacity across countries. This should include advocating phased implementation where justified, alongside technical cooperation, knowledge sharing and capacity-building to help industries adapt to the new requirements.  And finally, industry will have to take greater ownership of domestic preparedness. Investments today in supply chain due diligence, MRV traceability, emissions measurement, product-level data systems, and certifications standards will only help make Indian industry future-ready. Industry associations can further support micro, small and medium-sized enterprises by developing shared compliance platforms and providing technical assistance to help them meet evolving regulatory requirements.
The writers are, respectively, a policy fellow at the Grantham Research Institute at the London School of Economics and a Mumbai-based economist     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Watch for El Nino's delayed fallout
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Watch for El Nino's delayed falloutWatch for El Nino's delayed fallout

Modest decline in sown area masks risks to crop yields and rural incomes

premium

El Niño and deficient monsoon rainfall threaten kharif yields, rural incomes and India’s economic growth in the second half of FY27

Nikhil Gupta6 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 10:23 PM ISTDespite a super El Nino and a 12.6 per cent rainfall deficit during the recently concluded Southwest monsoon, the area sown under food grains and oilseeds in the 2026 kharif season declined by just 1.2 per cent year-on-year (YoY). In fact, the area sown remained about 2 per cent above normal. Does this suggest that the adverse economic impact of El Nino will be muted this year? Some market participants certainly seem to think so. I beg to differ, however, for good reason.  It is important to note that the area sown during the kharif season doesn’t change much year-on-year. Based on data for the past 26 years (2000-2025), the average fall in kharif area sown during rainfall-deficit years (about -10 per cent or worse) was only 0.9 per cent. There were eight such years in the period: FY01, FY03, FY05, FY10, FY15, FY16, FY19 and FY24. During moderate or strong El Nino years (only four episodes in FY03, FY10, FY16 and FY24), kharif area sown was down by an average of 1.9 per cent. The average growth in kharif area sown was under 1 per cent during normal (non-El Nino or non-rainfall-deficit) years. The fall of 1.2 per cent in 2026, therefore, is not out of line.  Notwithstanding a small fall in area sown, kharif yield declined by an average of 6.5 per cent during rainfall-deficit years and as much as 8.4 per cent per annum during El Nino years. In contrast, the yield under kharif season grew by 4-6 per cent per annum during normal years. Because of lower yield (due to low water supply and/or higher temperature), the agricultural output under kharif season fell by about 7 per cent annually during rainfall deficit years and as much as 10 per cent per annum during El Nino episodes. This compares with an average growth of 5-7 per cent during normal years.  Not surprisingly, then, real agricultural gross value added (GVA) witnessed an average decline of 0.3 per cent per annum during rainfall-deficit years, with the fall rising to about 1 per cent during El Nino years. During normal years, real agricultural GVA growth averaged 4-5 per cent. Most interestingly, the adverse impact on the real agricultural GVA during El Nino or rainfall-deficit years was entirely concentrated in the second half of the year (2H). For instance, while average growth in the first half of rainfall-deficit years was 2 per cent (and 1 per cent during El Nino years), real agricultural GVA declined by about 2 per cent per annum during the affected period. In the first quarter of 2026-27 (1QFY27), real agricultural GVA grew 3.6 per cent Y-o-Y; however, as yields get adversely affected, we expect it to soften towards 2 per cent Y-o-Y in Q2, before easing to 0.4 per cent in 2HFY27 (not a decline). This will mean a growth of 1.4 per cent in FY27 vs 3 per cent in FY26.  Not only real agricultural GVA but rural income (or wage growth) also gets adversely affected. Based on monthly data available from the Labour Bureau, real rural wage growth was 0.5 per cent per annum during the rainfall-deficit years (and 0.9 per cent annually during El Nino years), only about a quarter of the 1.8 per cent per annum growth during normal years.  Unsurprisingly, the adverse impact was more pronounced in agricultural wages (only about a fifth of the normal-period average) than non-agricultural wages (about half of the normal-period average). In the first five months of FY27 (April-August), real rural wage growth averaged 0.6 per cent Y-o-Y, with only 0.3 per cent growth in agricultural activities and 0.9 per cent growth in non-agricultural activities.  Further, real private final consumption expenditure has also seen slower growth in the affected years — an average growth of 5.5 per cent per annum vs 6 per cent during normal years.  Surprisingly though, the effect on food inflation is not so clear. While it has been higher during El Nino years, the adverse impact during all rainfall-deficit years is not as prominent.  Overall, a fall of 1.2 per cent Y-o-Y in area sown under kharif crops is not reliable evidence to suggest no adverse impact of El Nino. With a similar fall in area sown, we have seen a sharp fall in yield, and thus production, during bad monsoon years earlier.    What about improved irrigation levels or the declining share of agriculture in GVA and, consequently, in GDP? Irrigated area has increased across various crops; however, it remains low. About 70 per cent of the area under rice cultivation was irrigated in 2023-24, compared with 60 per cent a decade earlier and about 55 per cent in the mid-2000s. Similarly, about 35 per cent of the area under pulses was irrigated, compared with 20 per cent a decade earlier. This is one of the reasons why we don’t expect a decline in real agricultural GVA in FY27, despite a super El Nino and a large rainfall deficit.  Moreover, while the share of crops in the total agricultural GVA was falling from 65 per cent in FY12/FY13 to 54 per cent in FY24 (under the 2011-12 base), it was revised upwards to 62 per cent in FY23 under the new 2022-23 base and has remained unchanged through FY25.  To conclude, we firmly believe that the adverse impact of El Nino and a large rainfall deficit will be visible in 2HFY27. That’s why, we find it really difficult to believe that real GVA/GDP growth could stay at 6.8-6.9 per cent in 2HFY27, as is suggested by the Reserve Bank of India projections and the market consensus. Including an unfavourable base effect, weak fiscal spending growth (since we assume that the government will meet its fiscal deficit target of 4.5 per cent of GDP), and the adverse impact of higher inflation on consumption, we believe that GVA/GDP growth could weaken substantially to below 6 per cent. This will also make it difficult for the RBI to raise rates after December, making this rate-hike episode a shallow one. 
 The writer is India economist at CLSA India Private Ltd and the author of The Eight Per Cent Solution     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Prospects of reviving asset sale
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Prospects of reviving asset saleProspects of reviving asset sale

The disinvestment journey of the past decade has not been impressive. How it pans out now depends on some key factors

premium

Illustration: Binay SInha

A K Bhattacharya New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 5:32 PM ISTThe Narendra Modi government appears to be on a disinvestment drive. This is happening after a slow and halting implementation of its policy on strategic sale of public-sector undertakings (PSUs) it had announced in 2021.   Last week, the Union Cabinet approved a proposal to sell over 30 per cent of the government’s total equity in IDBI Bank at a price that should yield the central exchequer a disinvestment receipt of over ₹26,500 crore in the current year. With more than five months to go before the current year ends, the government will have collected more than its annual target of ₹80,000 crore from such asset sales during 2026-27. Equally important, the IDBI Bank deal means that the Modi government has now given a push to privatisation after a pause.  It is also important to note that the IDBI Bank privatisation doesn’t appear to be a flash in the pan. According to the finance ministry, the government plans to list three more PSUs on the stock exchange — India Infrastructure Finance Company Ltd (IIFCL), Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd (MCL) and South Eastern Coalfields Ltd (SECL). Listing MCL and SECL may not result in any disinvestment receipts for the government, as they are wholly-owned subsidiaries of Coal India Ltd (CIL), which alone will benefit from such share sale proceeds. But the listing decision on IIFCL, wholly owned by the government, will mean more disinvestment receipt if it is listed before March 2027 as planned. Indeed, preparations for an initial public offer of IIFCL shares have already begun.   To be sure, the government’s track record on privatisation so far has been unimpressive. After formulating a policy on strategic disinvestment in 2021, wherein the government decided to exit all PSUs barring a few strategic ones, only Air India, Ferro Scrap Nigam, Neelachal Ispat Nigam and Indian Medicines Pharmaceuticals Corporation have been privatised. Air India was a high-profile company, but owing to its huge, accumulated debt, the net proceeds for the government from its privatisation in January 2022 were only ₹2,700 crore.   Not that the sale of the other three companies saw higher realisation. The privatisation of Ferro Scrap and Neelachal Ispat yielded zero receipts. The sale proceed from Indian Medicines Pharmaceuticals Corporation was ₹118.73 crore. That meant four cases of privatisation got the government only ₹2,818.73 crore. Critics of the government’s privatisation policy have not yet latched on to this number, but when they do, reservations about the policy on strategic sale of PSUs will only get more serious.   In the last twelve and a half years of the Modi government, total disinvestment receipts are estimated at ₹4.37 trillion, of which privatisation proceeds account for a tiny proportion of just 0.64 per cent, with the remaining amount being collected through the sale of minority shares. In the last one and a half years, asset monetisation (or the sale of land and buildings owned by government-owned PSUs) has picked up, with a total amount estimated at ₹34,787 crore. Even after including asset monetisation, total disinvestment proceeds in the Modi regime so far have been less than PSU dividend receipts of ₹5.32 trillion during this period.   This is perhaps one of the reasons for the government slowing down its disinvestment programme from 2021-22, ironically the same year when the government announced its policy on strategic sale of PSUs. It was argued by senior finance ministry functionaries then that value maximisation  was as important an objective in managing PSU assets as achieving disinvestment targets. This reflected a shift in strategy that was no longer overly dependent on strategic disinvestment and required a broader and more holistic approach decoupled from fiscal management.   Not surprisingly, the change in approach was visible in slowing disinvestment receipts, rising dividends from PSUs, and a sharp increase in the government’s equity contribution and loans released to PSUs in subsequent years. Between 2021-22 and 2025-26, disinvestment receipts were estimated at just about 21 per cent of the total such proceeds during the twelve and a half years of the Modi government. In the same period, however, PSU dividends rose to ₹3.35 trillion, accounting for 63 per cent of total received by the government. And the government’s equity and loans to PSUs in this period rose to ₹21.45 trillion, over 57 per cent of what was allocated from 2014-15 to 2026-27. It was during the same period that the government’s Budget documents stopped referring to disinvestment in its capital receipts calculations. In what seemed to be part of its plan to de-emphasise disinvestment, all receipts from asset sales were classified as non-debt capital receipts.    Now that the government’s approach to disinvestment is changing, it will be important to keep track of a few parameters of the government’s receipts and expenditure allocations. One, it will be helpful if disinvestment receipts and asset monetisation receipts are clearly identified in the receipts budget, so that these numbers can be easily identified and subjected to analysis and dissemination.  Two, tracking disinvestment numbers will be important. But equally important will be the need to measure the pace at which the government is investing in PSUs through equity contribution and loans. In the early years of the Modi government, the amount allocated for equity and loans to PSUs was a little more than a third of the government’s total capital expenditure budget. In the last few years, this share has been close to 50 per cent. This trend should be reversed without any decline in the government’s overall capex target.   Three, it will be necessary to keep a close watch on the ratio between the government’s total receipts from PSUs (through disinvestment and dividend income) and the amount it spends on them through equity and loans. In the last five years, the amount of government receipts from PSUs as a share of total spending on PSUs has steadily fallen from around 30 per cent in 2021-22 to 15 per cent in 2024-25, before recovering a bit to about 26 per cent in 2025-26. This ratio should get better over time as the government’s disinvestment receipts increase and the need for fresh equity infusion declines.     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India has expanded higher education. Now it must build on it
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India has expanded higher education. Now it must build on itIndia has expanded higher education. Now it must build on it

India must address faculty vacancies, skills gaps and examination flaws to make educational opportunity more equitable

premium

Students at a higher education institution in India, representing the need for equitable access and examination reforms.

Soumya Kanti GhoshShashidharan Sharma7 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 10:37 PM ISTIndia’s higher education map has changed significantly in the last 12 years. Higher education infrastructure is proliferating. As of financial year 2023-24 (FY24), India had 1,289 universities, 48,246 colleges and 15,221 stand-alone institutes, an average growth of 47 per cent over FY14. Reported teachers increased from about 1.37 million to 1.73 million, while women’s share of the teaching workforce rose from 39 per cent to 45 per cent. The share of scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and other backward classes (SC, ST, OBC) jumped to 45 per cent from 32 per cent a decade back. Total enrolment reached 45 million in 2023–24, against 34.2 million in 2014–15, of which PhD enrolment stood at 344,000, with women accounting for almost 50 per cent. SC, ST and OBC enrolment was at 62 per cent in FY24 and girls outnumbered boys in science stream.   The Centre also expanded the premier network. The total number of Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs) and National Institutes of Technology (NITs) have expanded from 59 in FY14 to 76 in FY26, with addition of seven IITs, nine IIMs and one NIT. The combined students at IITs and NITs stood at around 244,000 in FY24, against around 162,000 in FY18 — a 27 per cent growth. Using the same institutions at both endpoints during both academic years FY18 and FY24, core-programme enrolment rose by about 58 per cent across the same 17 IITs, 39 per cent across the same 14 IIMs and 30 per cent across the same 22 NITs. This is growth inside the institutions themselves, not arithmetic created by adding new names.    The composition of the classroom has changed too. Women’s share of core undergraduate enrolment at IITs rose from 8 per cent to 20 per cent during FY18 and FY24. At IIMs, women’s share of core postgraduate enrolment rose from 26.3 per cent to 37.7 per cent; at NITs, their share of core undergraduate enrolment increased from 18.4 per cent to 21.8 per cent.   Employers did not mark down the larger graduating classes. More students were placed at higher reported median pay (105 per cent growth in FY24 over FY16). The market still rewards technical and managerial capability when it trusts the institution certifying it. IITs, IIMs and NITs are therefore a benchmark, not a description of the college most young Indians attend. Thus, India has expanded higher education to the masses much faster than what one could perceive in the last decade. The time has now come to build on it further.  Firstly, a recent parliamentary committee report recorded vacancy rates of 34 per cent across all national universities, with the highest vacancy at the professor level at 54 per cent. We need to red­uce these vacant positions.   Secondly, actual Union expenditure by the department of higher education almost doubled between FY15 and FY25. Yet its share of total Union expenditure fell from 1.6 per cent in FY18 to 1 per cent in FY25. Higher-education institutions accounted for 12.6 per cent of India’s research and development (R&D) expenditure in FY24, while the country’s total research effort was only 0.84 per cent of gross dome­stic product. We need to target this increase to 1.5 per cent.  Thirdly, the 2025 Periodic Labour Force Survey found that only 31 per cent of people aged 15-29 had received formal vocational or technical training. It is a pity that while hospitals, factories, data centres and modern cities run on technicians, machinists, electricians, operators, care workers and logistics specialists, our social imagination still ranks the office above the workshop. Germany and Switzerland place apprentices inside recognised occupational ladders, while Singapore connects work-study programmes to continuing education. India should apply the same principle.  Fourthly, across private and public universities, affordability and outcomes differ sharply and there needs to be a convergence.  Fifthly, changes must be made for the National Testing Agency (NTA). The NTA was created in 2018 as a registered society but not by a dedicated statute. According to the Ministry of Education’s written reply to the Rajya Sabha on July 31, 2024, a total of 194 personnel were reported at NTA, excluding the director-general. These included 171 contractual or outsourced workers.  Meanwhile, the government, following the controversies of 2024 and the Radhakrishnan Committee report, has added senior posts and introduced district coordination, centre audits, command-centre monitoring and biometric exception procedures. The Public Examinations Act has now strengthened deterrence against organised unfair means. These steps matter.   China’s Gaokao examination system is useful not because it is flawless, but because it treats redundancy as part of fairness. In 2026, 12.9 million candidates registered across 7,981 centres and roughly 348,000 examination rooms, backed by about 21,000 reserve rooms; more than 14,000 candidates with disabilities received accommodation. Provincial administrations coordinate secure custody, monitored transport and storage, emergency planning, policing, traffic and health support. The practical lesson is to plan for the exam day that goes wrong. When floods blocked access in Anhui province in 2020, two papers were postponed, reserve papers prepared and local transport mobilised. However, we must also appreciate that by July 2024, NTA did conduct more than 240 examinations, serving more than 54 million candidates. In addition, in 2025, the Staff Selection Commission (SSC) conduct­ed 10 exams for appointme­nts to clerical posts involving 18.5 million applications.  We propose four changes that would make the examination system feel less like a black box and more like a public institution emulating the global experience, particularly from China’s Gaokao.   NTA needs firmer foundations. A dedicated law making it accountable to parliament and independent scrutiny, including CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General of India) audit. NTA should build a permanent team of specialists, technologists and security professionals backed by a board that is clearly responsible when systems or vendors fail.  Creation of a candidate charter to promise time-bound decisions on disputed answers, translation mistakes, incorrect scores, disrupted examinations and re-tests. An appeal decided after admissions have closed is no remedy at all.  NTA should publish an annual account of disruptions, leaks, re-tests, appeals, vendor failures and corrective action.   NTA should immediately move over to computer- based tests along the lines of the joint entrance examination (JEE), with multiple dates spread over morning and afternoon sessions and the best score counted over two attempts, say in January and April. The entire application process may be mimick­ed along the lines of JEE or even the SSC exam pattern.  Finally, for millions of young Indians, an examination is a bridge between circumstance and aspiration. Article 21 of the Indian Constitution protects a life of dignity, Article 14 forbids arbitrary State action, and Article 21A establishes that education is a constitutional commitment, not an act of charity. We propose that Article 21 be amended to support a right to free and fair educational opportunity. Free should mean freedom from fraud, discrimination and unreasonable barriers.   Fair must mean transparent rules, secure examinations, accurate evaluation and an effective remedy when the system fails. A student cannot demand a rank, but she is entitled to demand an honest race. Let us make a beginning.   Ghosh is member, 16th Finance Commission and PMEAC, and group chief economic advisor, State Bank of India. Sharma is economist, State Bank of India. Views are personal.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Growing cyber risks
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Growing cyber risksGrowing cyber risks

Threats call for stronger systemic safeguards

premium

SBI says its operations and financial performance remain unaffected and is investigating the source and extent of the exposure | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 9:58 PM ISTState Bank of India’s (SBI’s) disclosure that 3,897 customer records containing personal information were identified among about the 375,000  found on the dark web is a reminder that cybersecurity is no longer merely an information-technology (IT) concern. The exposed pieces of information reportedly include mobile numbers, addresses, dates of birth and loan-related details. SBI says its operations and financial performance remain unaffected and is investigating the source and extent of the exposure. But for customers, the concern is different. Such information can make impersonation, phishing and other fraud more credible. The fact that SBI was alerted by the threat-intelligence provider, the Defence Cyber Agency, and Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) also raises questions about the ability of large institutions to detect breaches themselves.  The risks extend beyond data theft. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data shows that digital-payment frauds account for the largest number of cases of bank fraud. CERT-In has also warned of attacks on non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lenders, fintechs, payment-service providers, and wallets. The threat is becoming harder to contain because artificial intelligence (AI) lowers the cost and time of attacks. Earlier this month, CERT-In issued a critical advisory in which AI agents accessed live systems and confidential records of Indian organisations without authorisation; none of the affected organisations detected the access themselves. Attackers are also using agentic AI tools for financially motivated intrusions. The lesson is that conventional weaknesses, including exposed credentials, poorly secured application programming interface (API), and excessive cloud permissions, become considerably more dangerous when machines can exploit them at speed and scale. The recent eMudhra certificate incident illustrates the wider problem of digital trust. CERT-In has warned that compromised private keys could be used to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. A weakness at any layer, such as banks, fintechs, cloud-service providers, APIs or digital-certification infrastructure, can, therefore, have consequences beyond the organisation directly affected. The regulatory response must consequently go beyond operational resilience. India already has cybersecurity and fraud-risk frameworks under the RBI, while the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, provides for notifying personal-data breaches to affected individuals. Yet the relevant DPDP provisions and rules are subject to staggered commencement, with the principal breach-notification provisions taking effect only 18 months after the November 2025 notification. This leaves a crucial gap in the interim. Informing regulators and reassuring investors are not a substitute for warning customers whose data may have been exposed.  It should be mandated that regulated entities notify affected customers promptly when there is credible evidence of a material personal-data exposure, without waiting for an investigation to establish every detail. Banks and financial firms should also be held to enforceable standards on API security, third-party risk, cloud access, and AI-agent permissions. CERT-In’s guidance on limiting agent access, isolating testing environments, requiring human approval for high-impact actions, and maintaining tamper-resistant logs should become part of operational practice rather than merely advice. India’s digital-financial architecture has expanded rapidly. Its security framework must now evolve at the same pace. The objective should not merely be to ensure that banks continue to function after an attack, but to ensure that customers are protected, informed and able to act when security fails.     Topics : Dark Web sbi cybersecurity Data breach frauds Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: A singular approach
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / A singular approachA singular approach

Pollution-control plans must be coordinated across north India

premium

Delhi’s winter pollution-control measures require coordinated action across the National Capital Region and stubble-burning districts to deliver cleaner air (PTI Photo/Shahbaz Khan)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 10:06 PM ISTThe administration of Delhi has been admirably proactive in invoking the first stage of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP I) as soon as the air-quality index (AQI) in the city jumped from 179 to 244 (“poor”) in a day. The first of a four-stage response linked to the AQI levels bans coal and wood burning (including tandoors used in restaurants and open eateries) and the use of diesel-generator sets except in some circumstances. This comes just under a week ahead of Delhi’s winter-pollution action plan, which restricts petrol pumps from dispensing fuel to vehicles without valid pollution-control certificates, bans outside vehicles that do not conform to Bharat-VI emission standards, introduces a 50 per cent work-from-home mandate, doubles parking fees to discourage the use of personal vehicles, and restricts construction. These norms will be in place till the end of February. This early response is a well-meaning attempt to control winter pollution, for which the city has earned a global reputation. However, its efficacy is still to be tested, given the onset of the paddy stubble-burning season, the precipitous drop in wind speed, the monitoring abilities of the Delhi government, and the Diwali fireworks onslaught, which has, inexplicably, not been banned.  But these are only some of the challenges in ensuring that the citizens of Delhi enjoy clean air this coming winter. To work, they need a far wider ambit of enforcement, which is beyond the remit of the Delhi government. Delhi is situated within a wider bustling urban agglomeration termed the National Capital Region, comprising districts in Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. Most cities in these states account for the bulk of the urban pollution in India. For Delhi’s winter pollution- control action plan to work, it needs administrations in these areas to introduce reciprocal plans. Beyond the standard restrictions on old vehicles and construction — which have not proved noticeably effective these past winters — there is no evidence of synchronicity in planning. The National Capital Region Planning Board, which comes under the Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, could play a useful role in coordinating pollution-control plans.  But this, too, will partially address the problem. The latest data for the AQI ranking shows that Delhi is not one of the 13 Indian cities listed among the top 20 most polluted ones in the world. That distinction goes to Bulandshahr, Pali, Mathura, Muzaffarnagar, Rohtak, Kota, Hapur, Bikaner, Bareilly and Hisar. Only Mumbai, Agartala, and Burhanpur (Madhya Pradesh) fall outside the northern Gangetic belt. Several of these urban polluters lie close to the stubble-burning zones. No northern city is immune to the dense smoke from fires that farmers routinely set to clear their fields ahead of the rabi season. So far, the governments of Haryana and Punjab — ground zero of stubble-burning — have yet to offer viable solutions to a problem that clearly demands intervention from the central government, as it is the result of long-term central agricultural policies. The bottom line, therefore, is that without a coordinated action plan that involves North Indian urban administrations as well as the rural districts, citywise pollution-action plans will prove largely ineffective. For the Union government, getting its act together is no longer a question of politics but of addressing a burgeoning public-health crisis.     Topics : Stubble burning Delhi air pollution winter pollution Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Safety first in road contracts
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Safety first in road contractsSafety first in road contracts

Penalty regime should be backed by rigorous project appraisal

premium

The government's proposed penalties for road construction defects highlight the need for stricter safety inspections and better engineering standards to prevent fatal accidents. | Representative Picture

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 9:48 PM ISTThe Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ plan to penalise contractors in engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) for deficiencies in road construction leading to fatal accidents marks a significant drive towards enforcing greater accountability and safety in projects. Contractors will be given an opportunity to rectify the error within 15 days of the first accident, with the option for the government to step in to undertake remedial work at the contractor’s cost if the person does not comply within the deadline. If another accident occurs within a year of the first at the same spot or 500 metres from the original location, contractors will be charged ₹25 lakh for each fatality and ₹10 lakh for each grievous injury. Though this punitive framework appears unexceptionable in theory, it amounts to action taken after a tragedy occurs.  The question is whether this move needs to be complemented by a more rigorous project appraisal and inspection regime within the relevant government agencies, to ensure that project design and engineering are optimum in the first place. In a country in which experienced contractors are known to display no mean talent in exploiting contractual weaknesses, zero tolerance should precede a repent-and-pay policy. India has the distinction of having the world’s third-largest road network but also shares with China global leadership in road fatalities. In 2025, India recorded over 183,000 fatalities from over 500,000 accidents, averaging 21 deaths every hour, according to the government data. Poor road design is not the only cause of these. Rash driving and rule breaking too are major contributors, but bad road design does constitute a significant threat. Former Tata Sons chairman Cyrus Mistry’s death in 2022 was partly the result of an engineering flaw on the highway on which he was travelling (though the driver, too, was speeding).  Still, the problem is clearly serious enough for the Road Transport Minister Nitin Gadkari to flag the issue. Speaking at a road-safety event in August, he identified poorly designed accident-prone stretches or black spots as a major cause of road deaths. He spoke of spending a steep ₹40,000 crore to identify the most vulnerable spots in 100 districts to fix the problem. Though this exercise is good, the question is why it should have been needed. The government uses a mix of models for road construction projects — EPC; the hybrid annuity model, or HAM, part-financed by the government; and the build-operate-transfer or BOT annuity model, in which the government pays the contractor fixed semi-annual amounts.  Typically, payments for road projects are linked to pre-agreed milestones and a portion of the payment is held back for a defect-liability period, which can vary from one to four years. This implies that some level of quality control is baked into contracts. Perhaps the question the government should also be asking is why such a high level of fatality-causing deficiencies happens when a third-party independent engineer or certifier has to sign off on the quality of a road before payment is released. National highways account for over a third of road fatalities. With large highway projects under construction, the need for significantly upgrading the monitoring of engineering and construction quality has become critical. The lives of thousands of Indians depend on it.   Topics : Nitin Gadkari BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Road construction Road safety road accident Road Ministry

Ambiguity on satellite communication is creating unease

premium

Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio Satellite await security clearances to launch commercial satellite broadband services in India, amid delays in regulatory approvals. (AI-generated image)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 9:46 PM ISTThe recent public spat between stakeholders on approvals related to satellite-broadband service in India points to a systemic problem. It started with Elon Musk, chief executive of Texas-headquartered SpaceX and Tesla, hitting out at potential rivals in India, calling them “oligarchs’’ and blaming them for blocking competition. He specifically insinuated that Reliance Industries Ltd (RIL) might have had a role in delaying the security clearance of Starlink, the satellite-internet company operated by SpaceX. RIL rejected the allegations, saying that it welcomed competition and that Jio Satellite Communications too was waiting for security approval. Bharti Enterprises Chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal joined the war of words, stating that his company had been in the queue the longest in starting satellite broadband in India. As for the Union government, Minister of Communications Jyotiraditya Scindia retorted by saying that India did not allow monopolies in any sector.  Bharti Enterprises-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, Starlink and Jio Satellite have all been granted the licence to operate satellite-broadband service in India, but they cannot commercially launch operations without security clearance from the government. Eutelsat OneWeb is reported to have got the Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) licence way back in 2021. Jio Satellite got its licence in 2022, while Starlink was able to make the cut in 2025. The fact that the companies armed with the requisite licence are unable to launch commercial operations is a matter of concern and frustration for businesses. Granting licences and then making businesses wait for the security nod, stretching over years, signifies an adverse regulatory environment. This is especially true when the government wants to intensify its reform trajectory, enabling ease of business and enhancing flow of foreign investments. To help realise the goals of satellite communications, the government departments and agencies must act in sync with one another rather than as individual power centres working in silos. While the licence — GMPCS — came from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT), other approvals for satcom are granted by the Department of Space (DoS), Ministry of Home Affairs, and security agencies. In the case of Starlink, it’s been under scrutiny over its alleged role in the Russia-Ukraine war through its communication network.  While the security checks have to be foolproof, the government must provide clarity on the process of approvals and indicate a timeline for starting operations. Some of the satellites engaged for the yet-to-be launched satcom services are fast approaching end of life, having been on hold for so many years. Besides security approvals, there are other deliverables as well. For instance, the Union Cabinet has to give the final go ahead on spectrum pricing. More than a month ago, the Digital Communications Commission (DCC) — the highest decision-making body of the DoT — set satellite-spectrum pricing at 5 per cent of the adjusted gross revenue (AGR) of a telecom company. For services offered to remote and rural areas, there’s a discounted price, at 4 per cent of AGR. This followed a long-drawn dispute over the mode of spectrum allocation for satellite communication. The DCC decision, based on the recommendations of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai), will have to be taken up by the Union Cabinet. India’s satcom journey, expected to benefit low-connectivity areas including rural and hilly regions, should not face any more hurdles.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Satellite telecom sector in India Internet
