entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Institutional stabilityInstitutional stability

India needs timely appointments in higher education

premium

Prolonged vacancies in top academic positions raise concerns over faculty recruitment, research and institutional planning

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTSome of India’s premier higher-education institutions are facing a leadership vacuum, with 37 of the 155 Institutions of National Importance (23.9 per cent) operating under interim, acting or in-charge heads, additional-charge arrangements or extensions, according to a recent Hindustan Times analysis. The problem is particularly acute in central universities, where 20 of 48 institutions analysed have an interim leadership or extended tenures. Some vacancies persist despite posts being advertised months or even years earlier. This is more than an administrative inconvenience. Vice-chancellors and directors oversee faculty recruitment, academic programmes, budgets, infrastructure, and research partnerships. Prolonged uncertainty can delay decisions on new courses, the setting up of laboratories, and long-term financial commitments. Interim heads may also be reluctant to undertake major reforms when their authority is temporary. Additional-charge arrangements compound the problem by dividing the attention of senior academics between institutions. Hence, prolonged vacancies can put institutions in “standby mode”, weakening accountability and long-term planning.  The consequences are serious because leadership gaps coincide with wider capacity constraints in higher education. According to an analysis by PRS Legislative Research, 29 per cent of the sanctioned teaching posts in central universities were vacant as of December 2024. For professors, the vacancy rate stood at 56 per cent. These shortages place additional pressure on existing faculty. The appointment process also needs closer scrutiny. The analysis highlights cases in which selection procedures had begun well before the incumbent’s tenure ended, yet successors were not announced in time. Indira Gandhi National Tribal University, for instance, had functioned without a regular vice-chancellor for nearly 21 months, although the post had been advertised in June 2024 and re-advertised in March 2026. Such delays raise questions about administrative efficiency. Disputes over search committees and compliance with selection norms can further erode confidence in the process. Transparent, merit-based appointments are essential to protecting institutional credibility and autonomy.  The government should begin selection at least six months before a vacancy arises. It should establish binding timelines for screening applications, convening search committees and announcing appointments, with periodic public updates on progress. Such reporting would make delays visible and strengthen oversight without giving the government greater control over academic decisions. Committees should have clear selection criteria, independent members and safeguards against arbitrary interference. Interim appointments must be strictly time-bound, with extensions permitted only in exceptional circumstances and accompanied by a clear explanation. Institutions could also have contingency plans to ensure that essential academic and financial decisions continue during transitions. Strengthening leadership continuity and institutional autonomy is essential to improving research, teaching quality, and India’s global competitiveness in higher education. Timely leadership appointments are a basic requirement for that task. Leadership gaps and an inadequate strength of teaching staff, even in India’s premier institutions, could seriously undermine the country’s broader objective of achieving higher sustainable growth and becoming a developed country by 2047.     Topics : higher education vacancies governance Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Improved closing auction
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Improved closing auctionImproved closing auction

Sebi should aim to increase participation

premium

Securities and Exchange Board of India | Image: Bloomberg

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:13 PM ISTIt has been 10 weeks since the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) changed the way the stock markets end their trading day. It introduced the closing auction session (CAS) on August 3, with the idea of giving one efficient price for index funds, large institutional investors, and derivatives traders. But, instead, it led to problems — especially for derivatives traders, who decided to stay out of the market because of the unpredictability and volatility during the end session. A new circular dated October 15 addresses the issues and is in the right direction. It has delinked derivatives from the CAS close. The notional average daily derivatives turnover is more than 200 times that in cash. Retail investors account for about 40 per cent of the turnover in index options. The CAS was putting all these traders out of the system. The problems should be fixed in December.  The issue started when the indicative equilibrium prices in the CAS system fluctuated wildly as algo traders entered and cancelled orders, which led to volatility. The CAS settlement price is directly tied to expiring derivatives contracts, where traders had limited visibility of how the market would move. Thus, most derivatives traders and domestic funds stayed away from the market during the auction window. The bigger issue was that cash trading stopped at 3.15 pm while derivatives traded till 3.40 pm. The final value for the benchmark indices that came after the CAS was many a time far away from the closing price at 3.15 pm. Likewise for stocks that are part of the derivatives, or futures & options (F&O), segment.  The volumes handled in the auction are about 1 per cent of the daily cash turnover. The auction filled well on days when indices were rebalanced. For example, on the day of MSCI rebalance there were many buyers and sellers in the auction session and volumes were at 22 per cent of the entire trading day. But in normal days it lacked participants and sufficient volumes. In comparison, on the New York Stock Exchange, the CAS handles 12.43 per cent of daily volumes, and the same is 10 per cent for the Nasdaq. In such markets, it is hard for any single player to move the closing price because the CAS accounts for more than 10 per cent of the volumes. In India, the volumes are only 1 per cent and a small player can move stocks and thereby the index in the auction session and make money out of derivatives trades.  The new circular addresses most of these issues. From December 7, the expiry session goes back to the previous 25-year-old system of volume weighted average price (VWAP) while the daily closing price of underlying stocks will continue to be determined via CAS. Expiring index derivatives will stop trading at 3.30 pm or the same time as the cash markets. The auction will happen afterwards (3.30-3.40 pm) but stock derivatives will continue to trade until 3.45 pm.  This is a return to the old system but the auction stays and sets the official closing prices. But the link between derivatives and VWAP is restored. However, Sebi is yet to address how to bring in more passive funds to participate, improve the securities lending and borrowing mechanism (SLBM) or short selling, or separate auction order types that exist in the developed markets. A working stock-lending and short-selling market would let traders sell borrowed shares in an auction where buyers are bigger in numbers, narrowing the imbalances at the close. Thus, there is more to be done. Most importantly, fix stock lending and deepen the auction pool.     Topics : SEBI Indian stock market derivatives trading Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

Rising AI-driven cyber threats, financial instability and geopolitical tensions pose growing risks to India's economic security, underscoring the need for stronger preventive measures. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 24 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page. 

 

The “two-and-a-half-front” threat now extends beyond military conflict to domestic unrest, AI-enabled cybercrime and disinformation, job losses and debt-fuelled financial risks, writes R Jagannathan. Citing recent breaches and attacks in India, Europe and Japan, he says India is underestimating how cyber vulnerabilities could magnify economic and political shocks. He urges a cyber alert, stronger prevention and dialogue to ease internal tensions. Jagannathan also calls for an end to the wars driving up living costs, reform of global institutions and compromise between political camps, warning that silencing dissent or romanticising street protests could deepen instability. Renaming the JD(U) after Nitish Kumar could signal a struggle over succession as his health falters, notes Aditi Phadnis. The party’s enduring strength lies in its EBC base, which helped Nitish build coalitions across Bihar’s caste landscape and made him a pivotal ally for the BJP. If those voters move towards Lalu Prasad, the BJP could lose its advantage; keeping the JD(U) intact and in the NDA therefore matters. With leaders divided over the party’s future and Nitish unable to settle the question, the Bihar leader's political legacy remains contested. Marco Rubio’s visit to Reliance’s Jamnagar refinery has prompted suspicion about US motives, but India should see its refining capacity as a strategic asset, argues Shekhar Gupta. The US needs capacity to process Venezuelan heavy crude, moderate fuel prices and serve its political and commercial interests. Meanwhile, India’s Russian oil purchases have not fallen, and are unlikely to. The Jamnagar refinery reflects how Indian entrepreneurs can turn scarce energy resources into global influence. Rather than distrust the Ambanis or reflexively oppose American engagement, India should expand refining and other industries and take pride in its business leaders. India’s public language is shifting from formal, Sanskritised ideals to Gen Z slang that names feelings and invites participation, observes Sandeep Goyal. Words such as “delulu” make self-deception playful and self-aware, while terms like “ick” and “flop era” offer quick labels for experience. Built for speed and remixing online, this vocabulary contrasts with the solemn, top-down language of duty and national schemes. Goyal sees the change as more than fashion: it reflects a move from telling people how to behave to giving them ways to describe how they feel.

Personal details can make fraud more convincing, while AI tools can exploit familiar security weaknesses at speed and scale. The editorial calls for prompt customer notification when material data exposure is credibly suspected, alongside enforceable standards for API, cloud, third-party and AI-agent security. Delhi’s early move to invoke the first stage of Grap is a welcome but untested response to worsening air quality. Its impact will depend on enforcement, weather and seasonal sources such as stubble burning and fireworks. Neighbouring cities and rural districts also need coordinated measures, with the National Capital Region Planning Board helping align urban action. Without this wider effort, city-level plans will remain largely ineffective, says today’s second editorial.  Despite a 12.6 per cent monsoon rainfall deficit and a super El Niño, kharif sowing area fell just 1.2 per cent in 2026, but Nikhil Gupta cautions against interpreting this as evidence of limited economic damage. Historical data show that yields and agricultural output typically fall sharply during El Niño years, with the effects concentrated in the second half. Gupta expects agricultural GVA growth to slow to 1.4 per cent in FY27 from 3 per cent in FY26, alongside weaker rural wages and consumption. Including fiscal constraints, inflation and base effects, he expects overall GVA and GDP growth to fall below 6 per cent in the second half. The European Union’s tightening steel import rules reflects a broader shift from tariff barriers to complex regulatory requirements covering emissions, sustainability, traceability and supply chains. Sangeeth Selvaraju and Prachi Priya argue that measures such as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and corporate sustainability rules are raising compliance costs for exporters, even where free-trade agreements eliminate tariffs. The book traces government incentives, charging infrastructure costs and consumer concerns, while arguing that hybrids could provide an interim route to electrification. Though India’s EV ambitions are clear, Mookerji notes, the book leaves the central question unresolved: what is the country’s concrete roadmap to an electric future?

entry.title: India's WTO moment is now
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's WTO moment is nowIndia's WTO moment is now

Along with other middle powers, India must step up to revive the WTO and help reshape its rules in the interests of the Global South

premium

India has an opportunity to lead efforts to reform the World Trade Organization, strengthen multilateral trade rules and safeguard the interests of developing economies. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Dammu Ravi6 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTThe World Trade Organization’s Global Trade Outlook, released in October 2026, presents a surprising headline: World merchandise trade volume grew by 4.2 per cent in 2025, up from 2.8 per cent in 2024. This surge has come despite geopolitical headwinds — the Russia-Ukraine war, the West Asia crisis, unilateral tariffs, and chokepoints in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. As WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala notes, nearly 72 per cent of world trade is still conducted on a most-favoured-nation (MFN) basis, reflecting enduring faith in the rules-based multilateral architecture. This optimism, however, masks a deeper reality that confronts a large number of developing countries. The case, therefore, is not just for a revival of the WTO but also for its urgent reform.

 Revisiting foundational principles

When the WTO was founded in 1995, the world was neatly divided into developed and developing countries. The underlying philosophy was to help developing countries integrate into the world economy with flexibilities built in through Special and Differential Treatment (S&DT) and consensus-based decision-making. These were foundational principles designed to prevent majoritarian manipulation and coercion through coalitions. Thirty years on, these principles warrant a closer look.  

 The rise of emerging economies

 The S&DT concessions granted in 1995 were well-intentioned. What was not envisaged was how economic status would evolve — some countries graduating, others falling behind. The last two decades have seen the resurgence of emerging market economies (EMEs). About 30 large EMEs today are the driving force of the global economy, accounting for an estimated $6.7 trillion of the $26.26 trillion in world merchandise exports in 2025. If services are included, the value rises to $8.75 trillion.  

S&DT, consensus and MFN: The dilemma

 Developed countries and EMEs together number about 60 of the WTO’s 166 members. The remaining members are low-income developing countries and least developed countries (LDCs), whose combined share of global trade is no more than 10 per cent. Making a separate category for EMEs is politically sensitive — it risks fragmenting the solidarity of the Global South and weakening its collective leverage, a fragmentation developed countries have long sought to highlight. Aspirational countries need greater flexibilities to meet development objectives while the poorest seek even greater concessions and market access, including from EMEs.  The way forward may be for EMEs to voluntarily forgo some S&DT flexibilities, each according to its level of comfort. If India shows the way, others may follow. India can credibly lead this transition even in the most sensitive areas. In agriculture, it can shift support from Amber to Green Box through decoupled direct benefit transfers in place of price-linked minimum support price-based procurement. Such decoupled income support — not linked to production, prices or factors of production — qualifies as Green Box under Annex 2 of the Agreement on Agriculture and is exempt from reduction commitments. This would ensure benefits reach poor and marginal farmers without leakages.  Accumulation of foodgrains far beyond the requirements of the public distribution system is a huge drain on the exchequer, besides encouraging the overuse of agro-chemicals and depletion of precious groundwater. The same principle can guide India’s approach to the fisheries subsidies negotiations — replacing capacity-enhancing fuel and vessel subsidies with targeted, sustainability-linked income support for fisher families.  Such transitions would give India the moral authority to argue for changes in the rulebook in the larger interest of developing countries. The ability to subsume a national position within the lowest common denominator of a larger rulebook is a skill India needs to nurture if it is to assume a leadership role at the WTO.  Similarly, the principle of Consensus, however well-intentioned, was inherently flawed. It presumed convergence among members despite vastly divergent economic strengths. In practice, even a small country can hold negotiations hostage and block outcomes, including Ministerial Declarations — as seen at the Eleventh Ministerial Conference (MC11) in Buenos Aires in 2017 and at MC14 in Cameroon in March 2026, where hosts had to settle for a Chair’s Summary. Some modification is necessary to prevent such logjams. The model used for the Trade Facilitation Agreement in 2014 is worth exploring: Members agree in principle by consensus, but implementation follows differentiated timelines based on each member’s preparedness, while developed countries take on obligations from day one.  Another pillar — MFN, which ensures non-discriminatory market access — has been undermined by unilateral tariffs. As Ms Okonjo-Iweala has repeatedly stressed, while over 70 per cent of trade still flows under MFN, the erosion is real. The long-term implication is clear: Countries will seek to offset MFN distortions through bilateral and plurilateral free-trade agreements (FTAs), a trend that does not augur well for developing countries outside the FTA architecture. While many will continue to abide by MFN trade, the new frontier is non-tariff barriers — regulatory friction, standards, conformity assessment, and logistics facilitation. Active Indian engagement here can help steer balanced outcomes in the interest of the Global South.  

Plurilaterals are integral to trade

 The plurilateral initiatives first proposed at MC11 — investment facilitation, MSMEs or micro, small and medium enterprises, ecommerce and gender — have become contentious. India’s position that these are non-trade issues is increasingly untenable. In a highly interdependent global economy, these issues are integral to trade. India has already taken commitments on them in bilateral agreements, yet hesitates to participate in multilateral rule-making at the WTO.  In fact, the New Delhi Brics Declaration of September 2026 has itself recognised the importance of identifying “appropriate pathways for plurilateral initiatives into the WTO legal framework”. Staying out is not an option — rules made outside by a critical mass inevitably impact outsiders. India’s participation can ensure balance and defend the interests of the Global South.  

The crown jewel: Dispute settlement

 The Dispute Settlement Mechanism, the crown jewel of the WTO, has been crippled since 2017 when the US blocked appointments to the Appellate Body. It was a major blow to a system seen as ensuring fairness and equity. The European Union’s alternative model — with mediation, non-appeal settlements and enforcement — could be a starting point. It calls for creative thinking. India’s long experience in trade disputes, both at the WTO and bilaterally, can add immense value in crafting an acceptable model for all.  

India can lead

 It is time for India to actively participate in reviving the WTO. If middle powers, including the EU, come forward, the chances of revival will brighten. Canada’s idea of middle powers leading the WTO's revival is worth serious deliberation — and India is well-placed to lead it.

entry.title: Rupee volatility is a signal
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Rupee volatility is a signalRupee volatility is a signal

The world is changing structurally, and India needs to adjust

premium

The rupee's volatility and declining foreign exchange reserves highlight growing pressure on India's external sector amid foreign capital outflows, rising crude prices and higher global bond yields. | Representative Picture

Rajesh Kumar5 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 10:02 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is fighting a difficult battle to keep the rupee stable. It is intervening in the foreign exchange market and has imposed several restrictions on currency derivatives to curb speculation. It also raised foreign currency through special swap schemes, including the one for non-resident Indians. The response to the scheme was encouraging, with banks mobilising about $133 billion through Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank), or FCNR (B), deposits. This helped take India’s foreign exchange reserves to a record high of $785.71 billion in the week ended September 4.  Some saw the mobilisation as an effort to build buffers in an uncertain economic environment, though the RBI had reserves worth over $680 billion when it announced the step. As things stand, the reserves have declined by about $60 billion from the record highs. Part of the decline can possibly be explained by revaluation to reflect the actual value of the assets the central bank holds. But it also suggests that the RBI is intervening aggressively in the market.  The RBI’s stated policy is that it intervenes in the market only to address excess volatility and does not target any level. However, in the present circumstances, it does appear to be chasing other objectives as well, perhaps to prevent the rupee from breaching a certain level. The rupee at 100 against the dollar, for instance, would make headlines and become a political issue. However, for economic policy managers, this number should not matter much. In fact, what should matter is that at the current rate of decline in reserves, the FCNR (B) buffer will quickly disappear. The FCNR (B) mobilisation showed that India can quickly raise significant amounts of foreign funds in a short period of time, but such an option cannot be used again in the near term.  At the fundamental level, what is needed is a dispassionate assessment of the situation and appropriate adjustments in domestic policies. One explanation for currency market volatility is the West Asia crisis and its sustained impact on crude-oil prices. This is a reasonable concern. With no clear resolution road map in sight, higher energy prices will continue to influence sentiment in the currency market. However, it is worth highlighting that India faced a balance of payments (BoP) deficit in the previous two financial  years as well.  India usually runs a current account deficit (CAD), which is financed by global capital flows. There is nothing inherently wrong with running a reasonable CAD. Foreign capital supplements domestic savings and is an important part of India’s broader macroeconomic management structure. Even the fiscal responsibility and budget management (FRBM) framework took into account the availability of foreign savings.  However, what has happened in recent periods is that India has not been able to attract and retain enough foreign capital. Foreign portfolio investors, for instance, have sold Indian financial assets worth over $26 billion so far in 2026. Thus, the issue is not limited to the CAD. In fact, professional forecasters’ projection— published in the latest Monetary Policy Report of the RBI— for CAD in the current financial year is 1.2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), which cannot be termed as alarming in normal circumstances. The bigger problem is the capital account.  So why is India not attracting enough capital? There are at least two explanations. First, increasing investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and related areas is absorbing capital from around the world. Since India is not in the AI play in any significant manner, it is unable to draw foreign flows. The AI boom is also one of the reasons Indian stock markets have underperformed and are witnessing outflows of foreign funds. Reports suggest that AI investment may be slowing. It is also being argued globally that investment in AI and the valuations of related companies are showing signs of a bubble. There is a view that once this bubble bursts, funds will get redirected to markets like India.  This sounds more like hope, and Indian policy managers must not buy such arguments. On the contrary, a burst or a significant correction in valuations could lead to considerable global financial instability, if not a crisis. Trillions of dollars are being invested in AI infrastructure, and an increasingly large proportion of this investment is being financed through debt and other complex instruments that are difficult to track. Experience shows that a substantial increase in global financial uncertainty results in capital shifting to safe assets, not emerging markets. Thus, a burst could end up putting more pressure on capital flows, at least for a while, and India must be prepared for it.  Second, higher bond yields in the developed world are affecting flows. If a global fund manager can earn over 5 per cent annually by simply holding US government bonds, considered to be the safest in the world, why take the risk of investing in emerging markets? However, this should have been anticipated. Public debt has increased substantially in the developed world, including the US, where it is moving up structurally. According to the International Monetary Fund, government borrowing requirement in advanced economies this year will be worth about 5.2 per cent of GDP, the highest since Covid. Public debt stock in the US is expected to increase to over 142 per cent of GDP by 2031 — up from about 109 per cent in 2019.  Thus, the world is changing structurally, and India needs to adjust. The playbook on both the current and capital accounts is well known. Leaving the adjustment reluctantly to the currency market alone could become painful beyond a point.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: IDBI sale revives hopes for stalled disinvestment driveBest of Opinion: IDBI sale revives hopes for stalled disinvestment drive

Today's editorials and columns examine Sebi's revised closing auction framework, leadership vacancies in higher education, PSU disinvestment, insolvency delays and a book exploring Delhi's history.

Illustration: Binay SInha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 21 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page. Sebi’s revised closing auction rules address the volatility and unpredictability that followed the introduction of the closing auction session in August, particularly for derivatives traders. The new framework, effective December 7, restores the volume-weighted average price method for expiry-day settlements and aligns the trading cutoff for expiring index derivatives with cash markets. Our first editorial notes that India’s auction volumes remain around 1 per cent of daily cash turnover, making closing prices vulnerable to manipulation, unlike in the US. While the changes restore a crucial link between cash and derivatives markets, Sebi must deepen auction participation, strengthen stock lending and borrowing, and improve short-selling mechanisms. Nearly a quarter of India’s 155 Institutions of National Importance operate without permanent leadership, with vacancies and interim arrangements disrupting decision-making, academic planning and research partnerships. Today's second editorial warns that these gaps compound existing faculty shortages, with 29 per cent of sanctioned teaching posts in central universities vacant as of December 2024, rising to 56 per cent at professor level. Delays persist even when selection processes begin well before incumbents’ tenures end, raising concerns about administrative efficiency and institutional autonomy. The government should initiate appointments six months before vacancies arise, enforce transparent timelines, limit interim arrangements and strengthen independent, merit-based selection to safeguard higher education and India’s development ambitions. A K Bhattacharya examines the Narendra Modi-led government’s renewed disinvestment drive, led by the recently-approved IDBI Bank sale, against a disappointing record of strategic privatisation. Four privatisations since 2021 have yielded just Rs 2,818.73 crore, while minority stake sales have accounted for most disinvestment receipts. The government’s growing reliance on PSU dividends and increased equity infusions and loans has further complicated the picture. With fresh listings planned, Bhattacharya calls for transparent reporting of disinvestment and asset monetisation receipts, alongside closer scrutiny of government investment in PSUs. The objective should be stronger returns from public assets without compromising overall capital expenditure. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code’s impact extends beyond resolving distressed firms, argue Aaraadhya Srivastava, Pratibha Kumari and Jithin P. Faster resolutions and higher recoveries initially strengthened lenders’ confidence, improving credit availability and costs. Research shows distressed firms took greater risks while improving operating performance, while import-dependent firms with more pledgeable assets increased capital-goods imports by about 31 per cent relative to comparable peers. However, rising resolution times threaten the framework’s credibility. With restructuring taking an average 1,026 days and liquidation 1,378 days in April-June 2026, the authors contend that timely recovery is essential to sustaining lending, investment and financial stability. Veenu Sandhu reviews John Zubrzycki’s The Shortest History of Delhi, a compact yet richly layered account of a city shaped by successive empires, cultural upheavals and competing visions. Tracing Delhi from its legendary association with Indraprastha through the Sultanate, Mughal and British periods, Zubrzycki blends historical evidence with vivid portraits of rulers, chroniclers and ordinary inhabitants. The review highlights his account of Partition as pivotal to the city’s modern identity, while praising the maps, photographs and informative sections. The book also critiques Delhi’s chaotic expansion, crumbling infrastructure and Central Vista redevelopment, portraying the capital as an unfinished, constantly contested work in progress.

entry.title: Not in default, but already affected
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Not in default, but already affectedNot in default, but already affected

Evaluating the IBC primarily through resolution outcomes provides only a partial picture of its effects

premium

In its early years, the IBC was widely credited with improving India’s previously dysfunctional corporate insolvency resolution framework

Aaraadhya SrivastavaPratibha KumariJithin P5 min read Last Updated : Oct 20 2026 | 10:48 PM ISTThe Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), a landmark reform introduced during the first term of the Modi government, marked its 10th anniversary in May 2026. Commentaries assessing the IBC’s performance have critiqued it on three grounds: (1) delays in the resolution process, (2) the relatively large share of concluded cases ending in liquidation rather than restructuring, and (3) the large haircuts suffered by creditors.  These are valid concerns regarding the functioning of the IBC once a firm enters insolvency proceedings. However, these very features determine what lenders expect to recover upon default and, consequently, shape the terms on which they extend credit before any default occurs. Thus, evaluating the IBC primarily through resolution outcomes provides only a partial picture of its effects. We, therefore, look beyond the insolvency process to examine how the reform affected firms that never entered insolvency proceedings.  In its early years, the IBC was widely credited with improving India’s previously dysfunctional corporate insolvency resolution framework. Before the IBC, creditors recovered barely a quarter of the value of distressed assets, while resolution often took more than four years, according to the World Bank’s Doing Business 2015 report. By 2020, recovery rates under the IBC had risen to over 45 per cent, while average resolution time had fallen to around 413 days, a remarkable turnaround from the multi-year delays of the past. This early period provides a useful setting for understanding the effects of improvements in the insolvency resolution process, before subsequent challenges weakened these gains.  Quicker resolution reduced the deadweight costs associated with lengthy bankruptcy proceedings, while higher recovery rates strengthened lenders’ confidence in the enforceability of their claims. With lower expected losses in the event of default, lenders had greater incentives to expand the supply of credit and lend at a lower cost than before. Research supports this argument.In a 2021 paper published in the Journal of Corporate Finance, Bose, Filomeni, and Mallick document that the IBC expanded the availability of low-cost credit to distressed firms.  Distressed firms, in turn, had an incentive to use their additional borrowing capacity to finance risky projects. Why? Because if such projects succeeded, the resulting improvement in cash flows could allow firms to avoid default. Consistent with this possibility, Singh, Chauhan, and Jadiyappa (2022), in a paper published in Finance Research Letters, document that the IBC induced distressed firms to take on more risk than non-distressed firms, with the increase in risk-taking accompanied by improved operating performance. These results suggest that a bankruptcy law that rapidly resolves insolvency, as the IBC did during its initial years, can both enable creditors to recover a larger fraction of their dues more quickly and improve the prospects of distressed firms.  These findings should not, however, imply that the IBC mattered only for distressed firms. The reform could also have affected the financing and investment decisions of relatively healthy firms. How? By improving expected recovery for lenders and making the insolvency process more time-bound, the IBC may have increased the amount of credit that lenders were willing to extend against a given pool of collateral. Firms with a greater stock of collateralisable assets could then have accessed additional debt to finance value-enhancing activities such as capital-goods imports, which can serve as a source of technological upgrading. We tested this hypothesis and found that, following the introduction of the IBC, import-dependent firms with more pledgeable assets borrowed more and used the additional funds to increase their capital-goods imports by about 31 per cent relative to otherwise comparable firms.  Put together, these findings suggest that the IBC has consequences even for firms that never enter insolvency. Its influence, however, depends on lenders perceiving it as a credible mechanism for timely recovery. Recent evidence of prolonged insolvency proceedings raises concerns in this regard. According to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India newsletter for the April-June 2026 quarter, the average time taken to complete a restructuring process was 1,026 days, while the average liquidation process took 1,378 days. Such delays may undermine lenders’ confidence in the framework, with implications for the supply and cost of credit. Weaker confidence could, in turn, affect firms’ access to external finance, constrain investment by viable firms, and increase the likelihood of default among financially weaker firms.  The IBC should, therefore, be judged not only by what happens when firms default, but also by how the prospect of default shapes the behaviour of firms and lenders before it occurs. Its greatest contribution may lie not in resolving insolvency after the fact, but in changing behaviour before it does. For that to happen, however, the promise of timely resolution must remain credible.
